answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: The proposed Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula does not address the emissions impact from actions that produce incremental emissions, such as building a new natural gas-fired power plant to serve load. Instead, the proposed formula assumes all electricity projects are clean electricity projects. Failing to enable measurement of actions that both induce and avoid emissions will significantly limit the usefulness of the proposed framework.

answers.label: Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text: The full lifecycle emissions impacts of electricity projects - akin to upstream and downstream Scope 3 emissions – should be accounted for elsewhere in a comprehensive consequential method, if applicable. The electricity sector consequential method should focus on emission impacts that directly result from changes to the electricity grid.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: Calculating and reporting emission impacts for each reporting year, rather than estimating the entire lifetime of impacts at the outset of the project, best satisfies the GHG Protocol’s core principles of integrity, accuracy, comparability, feasibility, and decision usefulness by grounding the calculation in known, observable data.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text: The GHG Protocol should remain focused on accurate measurement of emissions and emissions-related metrics, rather than dictating the types of projects that qualify for measurement. Assessing the suitability of clean energy projects is the purview of target-setting organizations, such as SBTi and RE100. However, a regulatory requirement should be included as part of the framework – not as a test for additionality but as a threshold requirement for determining whether a clean energy project is actually voluntary.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
It is feasible to include a regulatory requirement – independent of additionality tests – because it is a necessary threshold requirement for determining whether a clean energy project is actually voluntary.

In contrast, none of the other proposed additionality tests are feasible because defining additionality through the GHGP's current process is not feasible. While we support the development of an impact metric, defining and incorporating additionality tests as part of the proposed updates moves the Protocol beyond its traditional role of measuring emissions. Aside from its conceptual and historical incompatibility with the Protocol’s mission, taking on the challenge of defining additionality creates significant practical difficulties. Underlining that challenge is that none of the additionality frameworks referenced by the GHG Protocol - UNFCCC, Verra, US DOE 45V, RE100, Ever.Green, and TCAT – share a common requirement, option, or exclusion for even one of the listed additionality tests (see section 7.2 of the public consultation document). This is because, in practice, there can be no universally agreed-upon approach to additionality. Different approaches to additionality reflect a subjective balancing of stringency, accuracy, and feasibility that reflects each standard’s perspective, needs, and context because the fundamental question – is this action additional? – relies on a counterfactual claim. The GHG Protocol should resist calls to codify one perspective on additionality as part of a measurement standard. Failure to do so will divert resources, delay work, undermine consensus, and ultimately reduce the usefulness, credibility, and scalability of the final revisions.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: Marginal emission rates can change significantly across a balancing area or even market zones. Nodal marginal emission rates should be required for consequential accounting.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: Hourly should also be the minimum required temporal granularity for consequential accounting.

answers.label: Appropriate margin weighting approaches
selections: Default 0.50 build margin weight for all projects

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text: Initially, a single, standardized weighting of operating and build margin (e.g., 50/50) applied across all electricity projects is the best way to support the consequential framework’s credibility, scalability, and climate-impact relevance. Such an approach is simple and transparent, highly comparable, features low manipulation risk, feasible to scale, and consistent with the Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-Connected Electricity Projects, which recommend a default 50/50 weighting. Subsequently, empirical evidence could be used to validate or adjust future default values, reserving project-specific weighting for exceptional cases or supplemental disclosures.

answers.label: Weighting approaches not feasible to implement
Why selected weighting approaches are infeasible
answers.text: Any approach to assigning build and operating margin weights that advantages specific project types (e.g., variable versus baseload clean energy) is not feasible to implement because of the inherent challenges to comparability, scalability, and manipulation it creates.
